title: Costs, buy and hold, and the vault
summary: Why costs matter, why every rule meets buy and hold, and what a backtest cannot tell you.

steps.head: Trading has a price
steps.body: Every trade costs a little, from fees and a slightly worse price. We count it in {{basis-point|basis points}}. 100 basis points is 1%.

steps.head: Small costs add up
steps.body: A rule that trades often pays the cost again and again. A result that looks good can turn bad after costs.

steps.head: Compare with buy and hold
steps.body: {{buy-and-hold|Buy and hold}} means buying once and doing nothing. Every rule should be shown next to it.

steps.head: The vault
steps.body: The {{vault|vault}} holds the newest years, kept locked. You can open it once, with one rule, after you have tried that rule on the practice years.
steps.more: One look only, so you cannot keep peeking and adjusting until the result looks good.

steps.head: What a backtest cannot tell you
steps.body: A {{backtest|backtest}} tests the past. The future can be different. Nothing here is advice, and no result is a promise.

questions.prompt: Why can the vault be opened only once?

options.text: So you cannot keep peeking and adjusting until it looks good.
options.why: Right. Every look at the vault would otherwise become one more try.
No. The reason is not speed. It is fairness to your own test.
No. It costs nothing. The limit protects the test.

questions.prompt: A rule did better than buy and hold on the practice years. What is safe to say?

options.text: It did so on those years. That says little about the future.
options.why: Right. A past result is a fact about the past only.

options.text: It will do so next year.
options.why: No. Nothing here predicts next year.

options.text: You should use it with real money.
options.why: No. This site gives no advice, and a past result is not a reason to trade.
